title: High-Speed Amplifier Design
intro: The second study: a differential gain-of-4 amplifier with at most 1% gain error, 1 Vpp differential output, 1 pF loads, and settling to 0.5% within 5 ns from a 1 V supply, at the lowest power. It is the kind of stage a pipelined ADC needs (Razavi, Section 11.6).

blocks.text: A 1% gain error needs a gain defined by passive ratios, i.e. a closed loop, and the open-loop gain must then be large; with the 1 V swing, that means a two-stage op amp. With resistors,

blocks.caption: Gain 4 with under 1% error needs $A_0 \ge 500$ (ignoring loading).

blocks.text: Feedback lowers the output resistance and raises the bandwidth by the loop gain $\beta A_0 \approx A_0/5$. But large resistors would again put a pole at the op-amp input, so the feedback is made capacitive:

blocks.alt: Schematic. Vin drives capacitor C1 into node X, the op amp's minus input, which also has Cin to ground. C2 connects X to the output. The output has load CL to ground. The plus input is grounded.
blocks.caption: Single-ended view of the capacitive-feedback amplifier, including the op-amp input capacitance.

blocks.text: Capacitors add no pole of their own: $C_2$ in series with $C_1 + C_{in}$ simply loads the output. The response is not high-pass, since X has no resistive path; but X then has no defined DC level either (gate leakage drifts it to a rail). Large resistors $R_F$ across $C_2$ fix the level at the price of a high-pass corner $1/(2\pi R_FC_2)$; in a sampled system a reset switch does the job (see the switched-capacitor chapter). Note that $C_{in}$ raises the gain error: if $C_{in} \approx (C_1 + C_2)/5$ the op amp needs 20% more gain, so $C_1 + C_2 \gg C_{in}$ is preferred, at a cost in speed.

For a single pole, settling to 0.5% takes $t_s = -\tau\ln 0.005 = 5.3\tau$, so 5 ns needs $\tau \le 0.94$ ns, a closed-loop bandwidth of at least 170 MHz. Modelling the op amp as $G_m$ with large $G_mR_{out}$:

blocks.tex: \tau = \frac{C_L(C_1 + C_{in}) + C_LC_2 + C_2(C_1 + C_{in})}{G_mC_2} = \frac{C_1 + C_2 + C_{in}}{C_2}\cdot\frac{C_L + \dfrac{C_2(C_1 + C_{in})}{C_1 + C_2 + C_{in}}}{G_m}

blocks.text: That is, $G_m$ reduced by the feedback factor $\beta = C_2/(C_1 + C_2 + C_{in})$, driving $C_L$ plus the series combination of $C_2$ and $C_1 + C_{in}$. A real two-stage op amp also has its internal pole, so compensate it for the actual feedback factor: the loop gain $|\beta H|$, not $|H|$, must fall to one at the second pole $\omega_{p2}$ (about 45° margin).

blocks.alt: Log-log Bode plot. The open-loop gain starts at 500 and rolls off from a dominant pole at 0.01 times omega p2. The loop gain is the same curve shifted down by a factor of 5, reaching about one at omega p2. A dashed closed-loop curve is flat at 5 and rolls off near omega p2.
blocks.caption: Compensating for $\beta = 0.2$: the dominant pole can sit five times higher than for unity feedback.

blocks.text: The closed-loop response is flat at $1/\beta$ until about $\beta A_0\omega'_{p1} \approx \omega_{p2}$, so the second pole must be at the required closed-loop bandwidth (170 MHz), and the dominant pole near $170\text{ MHz}/\beta A_0$, a little over 1 MHz. The two-stage op amp of the previous page has most of the right properties; relaxing its compensation by about $1/\beta = 5$ means $C_c$ from 4.5 pF to 0.9 pF and $R_z$ up fivefold (950 Ω) so the zero stays on the second pole. Here the feedback capacitors also load the output, lowering $\omega_{p2}$, so the cut is not pushed further yet.

items: Values: $C_1 = 1$ pF, $C_2 = 0.25$ pF, $C_{in} \approx 50$ fF, so 1% needs $A_0 > 520$. For transient tests $R_F C_2 > 10\,\mu$s keeps the droop negligible, i.e. $R_F = 40$ MΩ (a switch would be used in practice).

A 25 mV step settled to 98.82 mV instead of about 99: not enough gain. Lengthening the input pair would add $C_{in}$; instead the NMOS cascodes (which set the first-stage gain, while the much higher PMOS-side impedance barely matters) are doubled in W and L.
The step was overdamped, so $C_c$ and $R_z$ were tuned down to 0.3 pF and 700 Ω: settling fell from 5.8 ns to 0.8 ns, far better than needed.

blocks.text: Trading the spare speed for power: linear scaling
Divide every width and bias current by $\alpha$: gains and headroom stay the same and power falls by $\alpha$. The load capacitance does not scale, so:

items: The output resistance of the second stage rises by $\alpha$, so the output pole $\omega_{p2}$ falls by $\alpha$.
For the same phase margin the compensated dominant pole must also fall by $\alpha$.
The first stage's output resistance rises by $\alpha$ too, so $C_c$ stays the same.
The zero must follow $\omega_{p2}/\alpha$, so $R_z$ is multiplied by $\alpha$.

blocks.text: Scaling by 2 gave 2.5 ns settling; by 8 the response was heavily overdamped, and retuning to $C_c = 0.15$ pF, $R_z = 9$ kΩ brought it to 4.5 ns, an eightfold power saving with almost no redesign. Noise and offset grow with the scaling.

With the full $\pm 0.5$ V swing the stages' gains drop (first stage 39.5 instead of 46.3, second 10.2 instead of 11.2), so the open-loop gain falls from 518 to 403 and the gain error exceeds 1%. Doubling W and L of the NMOS cascodes and the second-stage NMOS sources restores the gain but slows settling: the pole at the cascode sources (about 200 fF against $1/g_m \approx 690$ Ω in weak inversion) lands near 1.15 GHz, close to the unity-gain frequency. Adding cascode compensation brought the large-signal settling under 5 ns at 370 µW.

blocks.title: Gain error with capacitive feedback
blocks.text: With $C_1 = 2$ pF, $C_2 = 0.5$ pF and $C_{in} = 0.1$ pF, what op-amp gain gives at most 0.5% gain error?

blocks.title: Settling time constant
blocks.text: With $G_m = 10$ mS, $C_1 = 1$ pF, $C_2 = 0.25$ pF, $C_{in} = 50$ fF and $C_L = 1$ pF, find $\beta$, $\tau$ and the 0.5% settling time (single-pole model).
solution: Numerator $= 1 \times 1.05 + 1 \times 0.25 + 0.25 \times 1.05 = 1.5625$ pF²; $\tau = 1.5625\text{ pF}^2/(10\text{ mS} \times 0.25\text{ pF}) = 0.625$ ns.

blocks.title: Scaling a compensated op amp
blocks.text: An op amp with $C_c = 0.3$ pF and $R_z = 700$ Ω is linearly scaled down by $\alpha = 4$. What should $C_c$ and $R_z$ become, and what happens to power, the output pole and noise?
solution: Power falls by 4, the output pole falls by 4 (fixed load), and input-referred noise power rises by about 4.

blocks.title: Cascode-node pole
blocks.text: A cascode device at 56.5 µA in weak inversion ($\xi = 1.5$, $V_T = 26$ mV) sees 200 fF at its source. Estimate the pole.
